review: The way the game distances you from both the people you knew and the world you ran away from... That is brilliant.

Killing Time at Lightspeed: Enhanced Edition, developed by Gritfish and published by Green Stripe Snake, is a short but striking work of interactive fiction that uses a deceptively simple concept to explore isolation, time, and the emotional consequences of a hyperconnected world. It begins with an elegantly simple setup—you are a passenger on a spacecraft traveling at near-light speed, bound for a distant colony. What seems like a routine journey of minutes or hours for you translates into decades and centuries back on Earth due to the effects of relativity. As you sit in your cabin, the only link to home is a social media feed, where the lives of your friends and loved ones continue to unfold long after you’ve departed. The result is an experience that feels deeply human, melancholic, and quietly unsettling.

The game’s entire narrative unfolds through a simulated interface resembling a social platform. There are no traditional movement mechanics or complex systems—your interaction is limited to scrolling, reading, and occasionally reacting to posts. But within this simplicity lies its brilliance. The social feed becomes your only window into the world you’ve left behind, and as you refresh it, time accelerates dramatically. Minutes of your playtime represent years back on Earth. You watch as your friends’ lives evolve, relationships form and dissolve, political movements rise and fall, and technology changes society in both beautiful and alarming ways. The story manages to feel intensely personal even though you can do little more than observe. You are a ghost in the digital noise, present but powerless, an eternal witness to time’s relentless advance.

One of the most impressive achievements of Killing Time at Lightspeed is its ability to mirror the emotional rhythms of real-world social media. The joy of seeing old friends post achievements is undercut by the creeping realization that you are falling out of sync with them. The tone shifts gradually from light-hearted to haunting as each refresh of the feed carries you further into an alien future. The Enhanced Edition enriches this experience with a refined interface, achievements, and an atmospheric soundtrack that amplifies the growing sense of distance and loss. The music, a subtle blend of ambient synth and melancholy chords, perfectly captures the loneliness of being trapped between the familiar and the unknown. The writing, understated yet powerful, reflects on issues of identity, technological progress, and the disconnection that accompanies modern communication—made even more poignant by the cosmic isolation of its premise.

Visually, the minimalist presentation is deliberate and effective. The interface resembles a futuristic social app filled with status updates, news links, and trending topics, which makes the experience eerily authentic. You don’t simply read a story—you inhabit it through a medium that feels familiar and contemporary. The clean aesthetic keeps your focus on the text, allowing the emotional weight of the posts to speak for themselves. The game doesn’t rely on visual spectacle; instead, it builds its atmosphere through the passage of time and the gradual evolution of the feed. What begins as an amusing simulation slowly becomes an existential reflection on the speed of change and the fragility of human connection. By the end, the sterile glow of the interface becomes a mirror for your own detachment, blurring the line between fiction and reality.

Thematically, Killing Time at Lightspeed is both science fiction and social commentary. It uses its setting not as a backdrop for adventure, but as a metaphor for the emotional dissonance of the digital age. The concept of time dilation mirrors how technology distorts our perception of connection—how we can feel close to others online even as we drift apart in reality. Each interaction with the feed becomes a meditation on change: the rise of artificial intelligence, the erosion of privacy, the fleeting nature of friendship. You see your friends evolve beyond your understanding, their values shifting as decades pass in moments. By the time you realize how distant you’ve become, the people you once knew are long gone, their lives reduced to archived posts. The game doesn’t lecture—it quietly lets the implications sink in until the realization feels personal and profound.

That said, the experience is intentionally brief and limited in interactivity. Players seeking branching narratives or traditional gameplay may find the format restrictive. It’s essentially a digital novella, meant to be experienced rather than played in a conventional sense. Its impact comes from emotional engagement, not mechanical complexity. The choices you make—when to refresh, what to read, which posts to react to—are subtle but meaningful, shaping your understanding rather than the outcome. Some may find the lack of agency frustrating, but this passivity is part of the point: you are trapped, just as the protagonist is, unable to influence the flow of time or the lives of others. It’s a narrative built on inevitability, and it uses that constraint to profound effect.

In the end, Killing Time at Lightspeed: Enhanced Edition is less a game than a meditation—a quiet, contemplative exploration of time, technology, and loneliness. Its brilliance lies in how it transforms a simple interface into a vessel for storytelling, using familiar tools of modern life to evoke feelings that are deeply human and timeless. It’s a short experience, lasting perhaps an hour or two, but one that lingers long after it ends. For players who appreciate narrative-driven art, emotional depth, and subtle world-building, it stands as a small masterpiece of interactive storytelling. It doesn’t dazzle with spectacle or complexity—it simply holds up a mirror, both to the future it imagines and the present we already inhabit.

In 2042, the space frontier has opened up and people are traveling to distant planets, the playing character has undertaken one such journey that's only going to last half an hour subjectively, but in actual time it will take decades. Thanks to the "the Outernet", a slow, distributed Space Internet of sorts that doubles as a way to explain the limitations of the game itself, the PC will try to keep in touch with the friends and acquaintances they've left behind, using a couple of social media networks: a Facebook/Twitter lookalike and a Reddit analogue.

While only minutes may have passed between one tap the refresh button and the next, for the traveler, each one is worth months of actual time for everyone else, and the PC lives vicariously through snapshots of life taken so far apart from one another, while Transhumanism gets kickstarted and then blooms.

If this is reminiscent of Einstein's Traveling Twins Thought Experiment, that'd be no coincidence, of course, but it still makes for a highly intriguing premise.

From a strictly mechanical standpoint, Killing Time is a visual novel, where the player will be mostly tasked with reading, although there is some light interaction that can change some outcomes and unlock achievements.

Despite its cool but minimalist retro looks, quietly brooding cy-mbient soundtrack, and cleverness in the writing, the game doesn't manage to be fully satisfying. Turning some version of the Internet and social networking into the main mean of interaction has been shown to be a tricky exercise, and many other games that have tried, have clashed against the difficulty of translating it into an unobtrusive channel to deliver their goods.

All in all, it's an interesting game, but others were able to accomplished more with the material, both when it comes to exploring transhumanist themes, and using them as lenses through which to look at contemporary life.

As a sidenote, and despite this being a relatively short experience, albeit with some replay value, lack of any kind of save function in a 2016 game is in my opinion inexcusable.

How short an experience depends on how much time you spend reading all that is available, BTW. You can literally burn through it or take your own sweet time - I'd suggest a middle-of-the-road approach: it's a "thinking man" kind of experience so it wants you to connect some dots, but nothing stops you from coming back and pay closer attention, if it turns out you like it well enough.

Killing Time also has more than its fair share of typos and mistakes especially in the early stages, a disappointment for any game, but more for a visual novel.

Final rating: Recommended, with reservations.

I mostly enjoyed my time with this interactive book - and that's a very deliberate choice of words. This book starts with a fascinating premise: as you speed away to a new life on a distant planet at speeds faster than light itself, you browse your old social media feeds back on Earth..with a catch. FTL travel comes at the cost of time dilation, letting you experience 29 years in 29 minutes, and isolating you completely from your friends stuck back on Earth. 

With this idea planted in your head, the player has little to do but refresh their social feed and see how the future unfolds. Through the lens of social media (and the trouble that brings...) you are allowed to explore the potential philosophical and social cliff edges we will soon face in AI and civil rights, guided by mostly good writing. At times, news posts were dense, and some of the content confusingly worded. There is no other gameplay, which is unfortunately the main sticking point for me, as is the ironic fall of the game into the very echo-chamber that it cleverly lampoons: by the end you are only permitted to see the world you have left behind through the very specific social lens of your Friendpage friends. I don't mind politics, but I can't help but think that it was a missed opportunity to explore the conflict that rapid changes in civic rights, the reach of corporations, and AI advancements could have sparked. Perhaps this was all intended by the devs, but it left me wanting more. 

Either way, I was forced to think, so the devs can chalk this up as a success. I like the idea, and the integration into an interactive art installation, but I wish they had been bolder. For those who need a bit more 'game' in their gameplay, this may not be for you.

[h1]29 years of social media in the blink of an eye. [/h1]

Killing Time at Lightspeed is (at a stretch) a text adventure game developed by Gritfish. It was originally developed for a game jam, and the ‘Enhanced Edition’ available on Steam is a slightly more fleshed out version of it. You are Jay, a regular ole person who’s on a 29-year spaceflight to start up a new life on another planet. It may only be 2040, but we’ve conquered the stars. The 29-year spaceflight will only feel like 30 minutes to Jay, but 30 minutes is a long time, and what better way to kill that time than by browsing social media. You’ll spend your time with this game looking through a fictional social media feed populated by your friends from back home, as well as looking at all the latest headlines. Each time you refresh your feed, you jump forward 2 years. 

[h1]Positives: [/h1]
[list][*]I quite like the presentation of the game. It has that computer console feeling to it and I think it works well. The character portraits are all well done, and there’s also some nice art at the beginning and end of the game.

[*]The writing is good for the majority of the game. All of these little posts are bite-sized pieces of a person’s life, and the devs did a good job of making it feel like that. Everything fits nicely together and there is actually something of a narrative to it that develops over the course of the game. Have you ever stopped to wonder about the unknown future? About the sorts of technological marvels we may or may not see? Those are the questions that this game asks itself. It plays with huge technological leaps made available in a not-so-distant future, seen through the one thing that is a constant and intrinsic part of most people’s lives: social media. 

[i] Killing Time at Lightspeed [/i] has you doing exactly what one would infer from the name: filling idle time. You’re a passenger on a transport ship to another planet. The flight itself takes many years, but thanks to the wonder that is technology, somehow your character only perceives minutes of travel time. Thus: “Killing Time at Lightspeed”.

All of the game is set to the tune of a sci-fi soundtrack that fits really well with the theme of the game. Only caveat here is that - at least for me - it sometimes restarts or cuts abruptly. The gameplay is simple: you click through an interface containing news and social media. On the latter, you can also interact with the post, by liking it or, in some select cases, commenting on it. If you choose to comment, you can pick one of 3, at most, options to answer with. Once you’re satisfied with everything, you refresh the page and get a new set of posts, news, etc. Here’s the catch, though: every time you refresh, [b] months [/b], if not [b] years [/b], go by. After all, remember: you spend years in a flight that you perceive in minutes, meaning that in the minute or so it would take the character to read new stuff, around a year or two go by. 

This makes for a very interesting narrative mechanic, as you watch your friends lives unfold, and see more technological advances happen, yet you are powerless to actually participate in any of it save for the odd comment. The result is a novel idea that has a sense of isolation to it. In a way, that sort of resembles the experience plenty have with social media, does it not? Lots of lives unfolding, told through a highlight heel, and in a lot of cases, you won’t be a factor in them, save for the likes and the occasional comment. 

As for more technical things. The settings menu is barebones, with just four options: display mode (fullscreen/windowed), zoom level, font (standard or dyslexic friendly), reset game. While the settings have some glaring omissions (as far as I could tell), like a volume slider, there are two accessibility measures that are [b] DEFINITE [/b] highlights that I wish more games took into account: varying zoom levels and an easier to read font. Also (again, as far as I could tell), you can’t save. It’s probably by design, but still, it stung a little to have to go and realize that I wouldn’t have my progress there if I closed the game.

Altogether, [i] Killing Time at Lightspeed [/i] took me 1h30 to finish, and is definitely an experience I recommend to anyone who might be interested in sci-fi themes or just reading/terminal-type games altogether. Also, if you are a completionist, this is an easy 100% achievement-wise. All in all, the game is not going to be everyone’s cup of tea (what ever is?), but it sure was mine. I enjoyed my time being just that: a bystander, getting glimpses of the characters’ drama and routine, killing time at the speed of light.

Killing Time At Light Speed is a great concept for a game. It uses the idea of time dilation - where time on Earth appears to pass faster than it does in your faster-than-light vehicle - to make the experience of reading the paper for half an hour into something that tells the story of a generation. The game looks the part, with its throwback monochrome UI and cyberpunky synthwave soundtrack, but the content just doesn't measure up.

Each "turn" you only get about 3 articles to read, and none of them feel like real dispatches from a future media organization. A lot of the articles haul out cultural references and social attitudes that are already dated today, never mind in 2050. I know it's a challenge when writing in-world media to make it not so filled with futuristic jargon and references to fictional people and events that it alienates the real-world reader, but this didn't even seem to try. I was hoping for a game that took its lead from the intriguing newspapers of Deus Ex or the deep terminals in CONSORTIUM, but this really is not that game.

I appreciate that the developer is trying to do something unique here, but I can't recommend this game to fans of sci-fi or story games in general.

There's something special about [i]Killing Time at Lightspeed[/i].  The player assumes the role of Jay, sojourning to a distant Earth-like planet Gliese.  But the year is 2042, faster than light travel is a reality, and they've only got a half an hour in-flight until you arrive at a new world.  While on board, the player undergoes the premise of the game:  Checking Facebook where every time the page is  reloaded, years pass by on Earth.

[h1]The Pros[/h1]
I'll start with the premise.  I checked this game out from the [i]Extra Credits[/i] suggestions of games I likely hadn't played.  I agree 100% with what they said.  The premise is awesome.  General relativity is something I don't often experience in games, but here it's the apotheosis of why you'll be spending an hour or two playing this.  In life today time is so important.  Multitasking and squeezing literally every second out of every day through the assistance of technology and networking.  In [i]Killing Time at Lightspeed[/i], time isn't a factor.  You can refresh when you want and skip through years of advancements on Earth through newsfeeds and viewpoints from your friends.

Next I'll say that the writing is very, very good.  This is a game with few mechanics.  In fact, you'll spend the majority of the time not moving your mouse or typing, just reading through a news article or checking messages that friends have sent you.  The themes cover just about everything in the field of science fiction:  Quantum computing, augmentations, data interception and throttling, advertising, privacy, cloud computing, climate change, mental illness, population growth, faster than light travel, cyber-terrorism, teleportation, terraforming, legal systems keeping up with technological advancements, gender and sexuality, classism, fake news, AI and AI rights, and more.  You'll also get extremely relatable "Top 10s" or "Trends we hated from the 2010s" popping up like a cancerous Buzzfeed article.  This game is by a small team, but the stories and articles come from a huge portion of those that contributed - and it shows.  Articles by different tribunes feel different.  Your friends respond to current events differently.  There was this hilarious article on an older man being a zombie because his heart implant got a corrupted firmware update, which your friends will acknowledge in your feed.  There's a touching AMA with a synthetic sex-worker.  It's just great, the variety and quality you get to sift through and read at your liesure.  At the end of the day, however, there's nothing differentiating Jay from you - the player - and it can be immersive to the point that it's emotionally overwhelming.

A final thing I'd add would be the soundtrack, which only consists of a few songs.  Though there isn't a lot here, the tracks are pretty dynamic 80s-synth pieces that really do capture the feelings I've got when I read about governments pushing for pro-machine rights or if a friend goes missing.

[h1]The Cons[/h1]
The aforementioned being said, I know that this title won't appeal to everyone.  [i]Killing Time at Lightspeed[/i] isn't much of a game, really.  More interactive fiction.  Clicking and scrolling to refresh your stream is all you really need to do in order to progress - regardless of whether you've read the articles or not.  If you're looking for action/adventure, you're not going to find it here.

The game can also feel rather restrictive.  There are lots of moments where a friend will ask how the player is doing, but there is no way to respond to it.  There's only select moments when the player can chime in to interact with those on Earth.  That and "commending", the equivelent of a like or +1 on social media, doesn't really seem to do anything but is available for everything that shows up in your feed.

The last thing is value.  This is a ten buck game that you may/may not get more than two hours out of.  It's pretty short, with really limited ways for the player to interact how the story plays out.

[h1]My Verdict[/h1]
[i]Killing Time at Lightspeed[/i] is not so much a good game as it is an important one.  It delves into all kinds of subjects form science fiction and at the same time makes in immediately applicable to the player through a lens of social media.  It's pretty brief, so I'd definitely suggest grabbing it on sale rather than full price, but if you want to sit back and hear a story told in second person, I'd have to recommend it.
